title: Texas DACA Recipients Face Uncertain Future as Protected Status Erodes
excerpt: With federal courts chipping away at DACA protections and the Trump administration deporting recipients despite valid permits, Texas Dreamers confront a narrowing path forward.
body:
• Texas is home to an estimated 90,000 DACA recipients who face growing threats to their work permits, tuition access, and legal protections
  • The Trump administration has deported DACA holders despite valid permits — at least one recipient was flown back to the US after his removal was deemed unlawful, only to be detained again
  • Texas has suspended commercial driver's licenses for DACA recipients and at least four colleges have blocked in-state tuition for Dreamers
  • Congressional gridlock has stalled any legislative fix, leaving recipients dependent on courts for protection

For the estimated 90,000 DACA recipients living in Texas, 2026 has brought a cascade of threats to the legal framework that has allowed them to work, study, and build lives in the United States for over a decade. Federal court rulings, state-level policy shifts, and a hostile Trump administration have converged to leave Dreamers navigating an increasingly precarious existence.

Deported, Returned, Detained Again

The case of José Contreras Díaz of Edinburg, Texas, illustrates the peril facing DACA holders. After receiving what he described as a "bait letter" from immigration officials in December, Contreras reported for a meeting in January and was arrested and deported to Honduras within days — despite holding a current DACA permit he had renewed for 12 years.

Three months later, after a lawyer argued the deportation was illegal, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement flew Contreras back to Texas on a charter plane. Upon arrival, he was immediately placed in a detention center for eight more days.

"It has been the hardest thing my family and I have ever experienced, and words cannot fully capture it. But I am home now. I got to hold my son, Mateo, and hug my family again."

— José Contreras Díaz, DACA recipient

The 30-year-old's son was born while he was fighting his deportation from Honduras. DHS says it still intends to deport him again, regardless of his DACA status. Contreras is one of dozens of DACA recipients the administration has deported, but one of the few allowed to return.

Erosion on Multiple Fronts

Beyond deportations, Texas DACA recipients face a web of state-level restrictions that are quietly dismantling their ability to function. The Texas Department of Public Safety has suspended commercial driver's licenses for noncitizens, including DACA holders — a move that cuts deep in a state where 1.1 per cent of truck drivers are DACA-eligible and the energy sector depends heavily on immigrant drivers.

At least four Texas colleges have blocked DACA recipients from receiving in-state tuition since a June 2025 injunction on the Texas Dream Act, curtailing educational access for students who grew up in the state. Governor Greg Abbott's office has framed the restrictions in fiscal terms.

"Benefits, licenses, and taxpayer-funded services should not be used to incentivize unlawful presence at the expense of hardworking Texans," said Andrew Mahaleris, the governor's spokesperson.

Courts Offer No Clarity

The legal landscape offers little reassurance. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled DACA unlawful in January 2025 but allowed renewals to continue nationwide. U.S. District Judge Andrew Hanen, who has long opposed the program, has blocked all new applications while permitting existing recipients to renew — for now.

As of April 2026, USCIS continues to accept and process DACA renewals for current Texas recipients, but that protection hangs on court-ordered stays that could be modified at any time with as little as 15 days' notice.

A federal proposal would create a Texas-specific DACA structure, tying work authorization to a recipient's address on record. Simply moving into Texas could trigger the revocation of both a work permit and lawful presence within 15 days.

Congressional Gridlock Persists

Despite bipartisan polling support for Dreamers, Congress has failed to pass any permanent solution since the DREAM Act was first introduced in 2001. Senator John Cornyn of Texas recently acknowledged the bleak outlook: "These young people who've now grown to be adults have found themselves in a very bad situation but don't see any prospects for immigration bills, including for them, any time soon."

The Texas Catholic bishops have pushed back against the crackdown. "It is contrary to the facts to claim that our state is harmed by DACA recipients lawfully working here," the bishops said in a joint statement. "This kind of unprecedented and disruptive action by our government will harm our communities."

For Contreras and thousands of others, the waiting continues — ankle monitors, court dates, and the persistent fear that the program that shaped their adult lives may vanish entirely.
nri_angle: The erosion of DACA protections raises broader concerns about the stability of immigration programs that Indian immigrants in the US also rely on for work authorization.
